source: Chen et al. (2025) DiffAdapt: difficulty-adaptive reasoning
finding: A small probe on the frozen model's last hidden state routes each question to an Easy, Normal or Hard strategy (temperature and max-token cap). At matched budgets it beats fixed strategies and saves tokens. Only small open models were tested.
numbers: Models 1.5B-8B only (Qwen3-4B, R1-Qwen-7B, R1-Llama-8B, Nemotron-1.5B, ThinkPrune-7B). Token saving vs Normal: Qwen3-4B 22.4%, R1-Qwen-7B 9.7%, ThinkPrune 10.1%. MMLU-Pro at 100% budget: R1-Qwen-7B 36.48 vs 30.71, R1-Llama-8B 39.90 vs 32.50. Qwen3-4B Easy-only strategy loses a lot on hard sets: AIME24 16.67 vs 60.00 Normal. Linear head instead of 2-layer MLP costs about 3.2 points.
limits: Main DiffAdapt results are plots only; the intro (62% reduction vs DEER) and abstract (22.4% vs Normal) headline numbers differ. No frontier model. Probe trained on math, transferred to MMLU-Pro. Gate cuts length, not a scaffold on/off test.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 stays open for frontier models. A learned difficulty gate is cheap (one pass after prefill) and works on 4-8B models, but the schema should not assume it works on frontier models.

source: Chen et al. (2025) DiffAdapt Table 11 oracle (Qwen3-4B)
finding: An oracle that picks the cheapest correct strategy per question beats every fixed strategy on both accuracy and tokens, so the headroom for gating is large.
numbers: Qwen3-4B accuracy / tokens. MATH: Normal 96.20 / 2662, Oracle 98.00 / 1279. GPQA: Normal 50.51 / 3022, Oracle 70.20 / 1001. AIME24: Normal 60.00 / 10672, Oracle 66.67 / 4429. Easy strategy on AIME25: 16.67 vs Normal 53.33.
limits: Oracle is an upper bound with answer knowledge, not deployable. Single small model.
agent_relevance: Always-on heavy reasoning wastes 2 to 3 times the tokens on easy items; a gate has real headroom, but only a good difficulty signal captures it.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Stop Overvaluing Multi-Agent Debate
finding: Five multi-agent debate frameworks on 9 benchmarks and 4 models usually fail to beat single-agent CoT or self-consistency, even with far more tokens. Self-consistency uses extra budget well; debate does not.
numbers: 9 benchmarks, 5 MAD methods (SoM, ChatEval, AgentVerse, EoT, MP), GPT-4o-mini and others. MAD beat direct answering in 34 of 45 GPT-4o-mini conditions but not CoT. EoT beat CoT on GSM8K and CommonsenseQA only with Claude-3.5-haiku. More agents (3 to 9) or rounds (2 to 4) mostly gave no gain. At comparable tokens MAD stays below SC.
quote: MAD often fail to outperform simple single-agent baselines such as Chain-of-Thought and Self-Consistency
limits: Exact per-method accuracies are in tables I did not extract; token control is by plotting, not exact matching.
agent_relevance: Directly relevant to gap 4: a multi-agent split (CoThinker) needs a token-matched self-consistency or single-agent control before its gain counts.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Heter-MAD results (same paper, Table 4)
finding: Mixing two different models inside MAD helps: Heter-SoM +6.4% and Heter-EoT +8.2% over the average of the two models run alone. Gains over a CoT average are smaller and uneven.
numbers: Heter-SoM vs CoT-Average average +5.8%; Heter-EoT +4.4%; others +3.6% and +2.1%. Per-benchmark swings from -10.8% (MBPP) to +32.9% (MATH).
limits: Baseline is the average of two models, not the best one. Benchmark-level variance is large.
agent_relevance: Diversity of the solver, not extra talking, is what adds value; a single-agent schema with one model gets no such gain unless it samples varied approaches.

source: Huang et al. (2024) LLMs cannot self-correct reasoning yet
finding: Without an outside signal, asking a model to review and revise its answer does not help and often hurts. Multi-agent debate does not beat self-consistency at an equal number of responses.
numbers: GSM8K, GPT-3.5: standard 76.7 (1 response); self-consistency 82.5 at 3 responses, 85.3 at 6, 88.2 at 9; debate 83.2 at 6 responses and 83.0 at 9 (read from a scrambled table). GPT-3.5 kept its initial answer 74.7% of the time on GSM8K; changes went correct-to-wrong more often than wrong-to-correct.
limits: Older models (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama-2); reasoning models today may behave differently. Equal-responses is not equal-tokens. Table row pairing is from text layout.
agent_relevance: An explicit integration or revision step is not free: at equal calls, plain sampling plus voting beat debate and self-revision. Any schema revise step needs an external check.

source: Lanham et al. (2023) Measuring faithfulness in chain-of-thought reasoning
finding: Replacing the chain of thought with filler tokens of the same length gave no accuracy gain, so extra tokens alone do not explain CoT benefit in these models.
numbers: Filler lengths from 0 to the longest sampled CoT, step 5 tokens; no increase on the tasks tested; TruthfulQA and OpenBookQA dropped slightly at longer filler.
quote: there is no increase in accuracy observed from adding " ..." tokens to the context
limits: One model family (Anthropic), multiple-choice benchmarks. Pfau 2024 shows filler can help when trained for it.
agent_relevance: Partial answer to gap 1: at equal length, content matters, not length. It does not show that an integration step beats other content.

source: Pfau, Merrill, Bowman (2024) Let's think dot by dot
finding: Small transformers trained with dense supervision can use meaningless filler tokens to solve hard algorithmic tasks they fail without extra tokens, so extra tokens can give compute with no content. Learning this is hard.
numbers: Two algorithmic tasks; filler works only with specific, dense supervision; theory ties usefulness to quantifier depth of a first-order formula.
limits: Trained-from-scratch small models, synthetic tasks; not prompting of frontier models. Differs from Lanham by setting.
agent_relevance: Length and content effects are separable only per setup. Token-matched controls are needed; a schema gain without them may just be compute.

source: Jin et al. (2024) Impact of reasoning step length on LLMs
finding: Making few-shot demonstration steps longer, with no new information, raised accuracy; shortening them lowered it. Length-without-content direction, opposite in spirit to Lanham filler.
numbers: 8 datasets. Zero-shot-CoT vs Must-Think-More-Steps: GSM8K 30.4 vs 65.8, MultiArith 40 vs 94, AQuA 29.9 vs 65 (as printed). Manual-CoT GSM8K 64.1 vs 76.1 with added steps; Auto-CoT 64.7 vs 70.1. Best row GSM8K 78.8.
limits: Table layout read from text extraction; the zero-shot baseline row values look unusually low. Older model, prompt-only, no token-matched control: longer prompt means more tokens by design. Gain shrinks on simple tasks.
agent_relevance: Supports the view that elaborated steps help weaker models; says nothing on whether an integration step beats plain elaboration. Gap 1 stays open.

source: Sprague et al. (2025) To CoT or not to CoT
finding: Meta-analysis of over 100 CoT papers plus 20 datasets on 14 models: CoT gain is mainly on math and symbolic tasks. On MMLU, CoT matches direct answering unless the question or response has an equals sign.
numbers: 100+ papers; 20 datasets; 14 models. CoT helps mostly symbolic execution but still lags a symbolic solver.
quote: directly generating the answer without CoT leads to almost identical accuracy as CoT unless the question or model's response contains an equals sign
limits: Prompt-based CoT only. Per-dataset numbers not extracted.
agent_relevance: Supports a gate: reasoning scaffolds should fire on symbolic or multi-step items and be skipped elsewhere (gap 2).

source: Liu et al. (2024) Mind your step (by step): CoT can reduce performance
finding: On tasks where verbal thinking hurts people, CoT also hurts models, and the hurt is not smaller for the stronger or reasoning model.
numbers: Implicit statistical learning (440-problem subset): GPT-4o direct 94.00 vs o1-preview CoT 57.70, a 36.3-point drop. Full 4,400 problems: GPT-4o 87.5 to 64.4; Claude 3 Opus 70.7 to 62.7; Claude 3.5 Sonnet 65.9 to 67.7 (no drop). Faces (500): Claude 3 Opus 44.0 to 29.6; GPT-4o 64.0 to 51.2; Claude 3.5 Sonnet 97.8 to 94.8. Exceptions task: rounds to learn GPT-4o 2.9 to 12.5.
limits: o1-preview comparison is across models, not same-model CoT on/off. Three of six tasks only; other three mixed.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: scaffolds can hurt strong models on pattern or perception tasks; the harm shows on top models. Crossover depends on task type, not only capability.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) The illusion of thinking
finding: With puzzle complexity controlled and compute matched, plain models beat reasoning models at low complexity, reasoning models win at medium, and both collapse at high.
numbers: Three regimes; accuracy collapse beyond a complexity; reasoning effort falls near collapse though tokens remain.
limits: Abstract page only; no figures read. Critiques about token limits and puzzle design not opened.
agent_relevance: Gaps 3 and 6: a crossover exists in complexity, the same shape as expertise reversal. Supports a gate on complexity.

source: Gao et al. (2025) Single-agent or multi-agent systems? Why not both?
finding: The advantage of multi-agent systems over a single agent shrinks as the base model gets stronger, and a cascade (try single agent, escalate if the output fails a check) beats both.
numbers: Table 2, original ChatGPT vs Gemini-2.0-Flash, MAS gain: HumanEval +10.7 shrank to +3.0; MBPP +16.0 to +1.2; GSM8K debate +9 to +0.8 (read from scrambled layout). Across 7 datasets MAS used 4 to 220 times more prefill tokens and 2 to 12 times more decode tokens. Cascade: up to +12% accuracy and 20% lower cost; routing math (GSM8K+AIME) +2% at 50% cost vs MAS.
limits: Pre-print; the two columns differ in era and model family, not one matched pair. Cascade needs a cheap verifier.
agent_relevance: Closest evidence for gaps 2, 3 and 4: scaffold value falls with model strength, and a verify-then-escalate gate wins on a strong model. Escalate only when a check fails.

source: Xu et al. (2025) Chain of Draft
finding: Asking for very short drafts (5 words per step) keeps accuracy near CoT at a fraction of the tokens on two frontier models, so verbose elaboration is not required for these tasks.
numbers: Date understanding: GPT-4o standard 72.6, CoT 90.2, CoD 88.1; Claude 3.5 Sonnet standard 84.3, CoT 87.0, CoD 89.7. Sports on Claude: tokens 189.4 to 14.3 (92.4% fewer). Abstract: as low as 7.6% of CoT tokens.
limits: Token columns scrambled in text extraction; only the sports token figures are read reliably. Small benchmarks, one prompt, authors' own evaluation.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: a content-light scaffold at far fewer tokens matches CoT, so length is not the active ingredient on frontier models here. Does not test an integration step.

source: Klepsch, Schmitz, Seufert (2017) Development and validation of two instruments measuring intrinsic, extraneous, and germane cognitive load
finding: Re-read. Three-factor model fits ratings; germane scale is the weakest. Study 1 N=97 (informed 48, naive 49); Study 2 65 to 95 per task.
numbers: Study 2 naive ratings: alpha ICL .81, ECL .86, GCL .67 with three items; GCL .85 with two items (support item dropped); .70 on tasks with prompts. CFI one factor .612 vs three factors .970 (RMSEA .071 vs .021; AIC 2185 vs 845). Pilot (N=27): six of nine germane items separated high and low tasks, d .36 to 1.68. Study 1 informed single-item alpha .25. GCL with mental effort r .32 to .41 (informed) and .51 to .77 (naive).
limits: About 59k characters of the page were not read, so GCL correlations with performance were not checked. GCL items ask about understanding and supporting elements, which overlap with comprehension.
agent_relevance: Closes the Klepsch part of gap 7. Confirms earlier numbers; adds that the three-item GCL alpha is only .67.

source: Bastani et al. (2025) Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning (PNAS)
finding: Preregistered field RCT with nearly 1,000 high-school students. Unrestricted GPT-4 raised practice scores and lowered later unaided exam scores; a guardrailed tutor removed the harm but gave no gain.
numbers: About fifty classes of grades 9 to 11. Practice: GPT Base +0.137 and GPT Tutor +0.361 (out of 1) vs control mean 0.28 (48% and 127%). Exam: GPT Base -0.054 (17% below control, p<.05); GPT Tutor -0.004, indistinguishable from control. First message only repeated the question or asked for the answer 67% of the time for GPT Base vs 37% for GPT Tutor. GPT Base students did not notice a loss; GPT Tutor students thought they did better.
limits: Math only, 90-minute sessions, paper exams; the Tutor could check answers in practice. GPT Base errors did not spill into exam errors.
agent_relevance: Closes gap 9. Agent analogue: do not let a tool or sub-agent hand over the integration step (the final derivation) when the aim is to keep the main loop's own state sound. A guardrail removes harm, not necessarily adds gain.

source: Bastani et al. (2025) PNAS heterogeneity and dispersion
finding: AI shrank the skill gap in practice but the gap came back on the exam; no significant heterogeneous effects on exam performance.
numbers: Dispersion (HHI) fell in assisted practice for both arms; no significant HHI effect on the unassisted exam.
limits: Details in SI appendix not read.
agent_relevance: Offloading effort removes the learning step; relevant if an agent reuses stored solutions without recomputing.
